6.AF.1.below: Define and use expressions with one variable and one operation to represent a given verbal description.
6.AF.1.approaching: Define and use expressions with one variable to represent a given real-world situation. Evaluate the expression for a given specific value.
6.AF.1.at: Define and use expressions with two variables to represent real-world and mathematical problems. Evaluate the expression for a given specific value.
6.AF.1.above: Solve real-world problems by substituting given values for multiple variables in a given expression.

6.AF.2.below: Use substitution to determine whether a given value for a variable is a solution to an equation.
6.AF.2.approaching: Use substitution to determine whether a given value for a variable is a solution to an inequality.
6.AF.2.at: Use substitution to determine which number(s) from a given specific set make an equation or inequality true.
6.AF.2.above: Solve real-world problems by determining which number(s) from a given specific set make an equation or inequality true.

6.AF.3.below: Represent a real-world problem using equations of the form x + p = q, x - p = q, px = q, and x/p = q for cases in which p, q and x are all nonnegative rational numbers.
6.AF.3.approaching: Solve equations of the form x + p = q, x - p = q, px = q, and x/p = q fluently for cases in which p, q and x are all nonnegative rational numbers.
6.AF.3.at: Solve a real-world problem using equations of the form x + p = q, x - p = q, px = q, and x/p = q for cases in which p, q and x are all nonnegative rational numbers.
6.AF.3.above: Represent and solve a real-world problem using equations of the form x + p = q, x - p = q, px = q, and x/p = q for cases in which p, q and x are all nonnegative rational numbers. Describe the solution in the context of the problem.

6.AF.4.below: Match an inequality of the form x > c, x ≥ c, x < c, or x ≤ c to a solution graphed on a number line.
6.AF.4.approaching: Write inequalities of the form x > c, x ≥ c, x < c, or x ≤ c to represent a mathematical or real-world problem with a constraint or condition.
6.AF.4.at: Write inequalities of the form x > c, x ≥ c, x < c, or x ≤ c to represent a real-world situation with a constraint or condition, and graph the solutions on a number line.
6.AF.4.above: Given two constraints or conditions within a real-world problem, identify or write a pair of inequalities to represent each. Explain each inequality within the context of the problem.

6.AF.5.below: Identify the parts of a coordinate plane and plot given points within the four quadrants or on the x- and y-axes.
6.AF.5.approaching: Calculate distance between two points to solve mathematical problems; OR represent the distance between two points on a coordinate plane using an expression, including absolute value symbols when necessary.
6.AF.5.at: Solve real-world and mathematical problems using order pairs or coordinates plotted on a coordinate plane.
6.AF.5.above: Solve real-world problems by determining multiple points that are a given distance away from an original point.

6.DS.1.below: Identify an appropriate display for numerical data including histograms, line plots, and box plots.
6.DS.1.approaching: Construct an appropriate display for numerical data including histograms, line plots, and box plots.
6.DS.1.at: Interpret numerical data displayed in histograms, line plots, and box plots.
6.DS.1.above: Draw conclusions or make claims about the data represented within histograms, line plots, or box plots. Use data from the graph to support the conclusion or claim.

6.DS.2.below: Define characteristics of a statistical question; OR distinguish between statistical and non-statistical questions; OR write statistical questions based on given information.
6.DS.2.approaching: Define appropriate methods for data collection; OR collect and organize data into tables or frequency charts.
6.DS.2.at: Identify statistical questions that can be answered by given graphical representations, OR make interpretations based on given graphical representations.
6.DS.2.above: Analyze graphical representations of data to answer statistical questions, draw conclusions, and provide reasoning for solutions.

6.DS.3.approaching: Given a data set displayed in a histogram, line plot, or box plot, summarize the data in relation to their context by:
6.DS.3.at: Given a set of data displayed in a histogram, line plot, or box plot, summarize the data in relation to their context by:
6.DS.3.above: Explain how a measure of center or measure of spread will or will not change when an additional data point is included in the data set; or create or complete data sets for given attributes and information about spread of data and/or measure of center.

6.GM.1.below: Identify an expression that can be used to find an equivalent measure in a different measurement system.
6.GM.1.approaching: Convert between different measurement systems in a mathematical context.
6.GM.1.at: Solve real-world problems involving converting units between measurement systems.
6.GM.1.above: Solve multi-step, real world problems involving unit conversions between measurement systems.

6.GM.2.below: Identify that the sum of interior angle measures in a triangle is 180 degrees and the sum of interior angle measures in a quadrilateral is 360 degrees.
6.GM.2.approaching: Calculate the missing angle measure in a triangle or quadrilateral when all other angle measures are given in a graphic.
6.GM.2.at: Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving the sum of interior angle measures in triangles and quadrilaterals.
6.GM.2.above: Solve real-world and mathematical problems involving the sum of interior angle measures in compound figures that are composed of triangles and quadrilaterals.

6.GM.3.below: Calculate the area of a complex shape composed of two simple polygons; OR calculate the area of one polygon within a complex shape composed of two simple polygons.
6.GM.3.approaching: Calculate the area of a complex shape composed of three or more simple polygons; OR calculate the area of one polygon within a complex shape composed of three or more simple polygons.
6.GM.3.at: Solve real-world problems about areas that involve the decomposition of complex shapes into simple polygons.
6.GM.3.above: Solve real-world problems about areas that involve the decomposition of complex shapes into simple polygons and include zones of negative space which must be removed from (rather than added to) the whole.

6.GM.4.below: Calculate the volume of a rectangular prism with fractional edge lengths.
6.GM.4.approaching: Calculate the volume of a rectangular prism packed with unit cubes with fractional edge lengths.
6.GM.4.at: Calculate the volume of rectangular prisms with fractional edge lengths to solve real-world and mathematical problems.
6.GM.4.above: Calculate the missing edge length of a rectangular prism given two edge lengths with fractional values and volume; OR calculate the edge lengths (and volume) of a rectangular prism given the number of unit cubes packed in the prism and their fractional edge length.

6.NS.1.below: Identify the positive or negative number that represents a given quantity in a real-world situation.
6.NS.1.approaching: Identify and interpret real-world situations that can be modeled using a positive number, negative number, or 0.
6.NS.1.at: Represent and/or compare positive and negative numbers in a given real-world situation and identify, interpret, or explain the meaning of 0 in each situation.
6.NS.1.above: Critique a representation of a real-world situation or explain the structure of a model that involves positive numbers, negative numbers, or 0 in a given context.

6.NS.2.below: Identify or write the opposite of a given number with or without a given number line.
6.NS.2.approaching: Plot 0 and/or the opposite of a given number on a number line, demonstrating the equal distances of opposites from 0 on either side of the number line.
6.NS.2.at: Identify and/or write the opposite of the opposite of a given number. Reason about the opposite signs of numbers, their locations on a number line, and/or their absolute values to justify solutions.
6.NS.2.above: Apply knowledge of the opposites of numbers to: evaluate multiple expressions representing opposite relationships for accuracy, or interpret and make claims about given generalizations. Justify claims and generalizations using symbols, equations, and explanations about the relationship between opposite numbers.

6.NS.3.below: Identify the location of rational numbers on a number line. Compare or order sets of rational numbers within the same type (integers, decimals to the thousandths, or fractions/mixed numbers).
6.NS.3.approaching: Identify or write inequalities that correctly compare rational numbers in mathematical or real-world contexts. Evaluate the correctness of statements involving the order or comparison of rational numbers. Identify quantities that are greater than or less than a given rational number. (New items at this level also mix number types — fractions with decimals.)
6.NS.3.at: Record comparisons using >, =, and < when comparing a set of rational numbers consisting of integers, decimals to the thousandths, and/or fractions/mixed numbers. Record comparisons using >, =, and < when comparing rational numbers in simple real-world situations. Identify a rational number that lies between two given rational numbers.
6.NS.3.above: Evaluate and explain comparisons of rational numbers with minimal differences in value in mathematical or real-world contexts.

6.NS.4.below: Solve simple real-world problems involving decimals to the hundredths, benchmark fractions and/or mixed numbers, and one or two operations.
6.NS.4.approaching: Solve simple real-world problems that involve decimals to the hundredths, positive fractions, and mixed numbers, including converting numbers into equivalent forms when necessary to solve the problem.
6.NS.4.at: Solve complex real-world problems that involve decimals up to the thousandths, positive fractions, and mixed numbers, and that require precise computation with a combination of operations.
6.NS.4.above: Solve complex, real world, non-routine problems that involve decimals up to the thousandths, positive fractions, and mixed numbers, and that require precise computation with a combination of operations. Evaluate the reasoning of or critique an argument involving the solution to a complex real-world problem.

6.NS.5.below: Evaluate numerical expressions for a solution when expressions include positive whole numbers and parentheses. Identify equivalent numerical expressions generated using one of the properties of operations when expressions include positive whole numbers and parentheses. Identify the first step in evaluating a numerical expression using the order of operations.
6.NS.5.approaching: Apply the order of operations to evaluate or identify equivalent expressions including positive whole numbers, benchmark fractions and decimals, exponents of 2 and 3, and parentheses and brackets. Identify one or more equivalent expressions by applying a mathematical property.
6.NS.5.at: Apply the order of operations and mathematical properties to evaluate expressions with positive rational numbers and a combination of parentheses, brackets, and whole number exponents, including 0 and 1. Generate equivalent numerical expressions by applying one mathematical property.
6.NS.5.above: Place grouping symbols within a numerical expression to set it equal to a given value. Apply the order of operations to evaluate expressions that may involve complex rational expressions (expressions in the numerator and denominator of a fraction), rational expressions divided by a whole number, more than one set of grouping symbols, or the distributive property.

6.NS.6.below: Identify the greatest common factor of two whole numbers when given a list of factors. Identify the least common multiple of two whole numbers when given a list of multiples. Identify equivalent expressions or analyze equivalent expressions using the distributive property to find a missing value.
6.NS.6.approaching: Identify the greatest common factor of any two whole numbers less than or equal to 100 and the least common multiple of any two whole numbers less than or equal to 12. Use the distributive property to write an equivalent expression for the sum of two whole numbers using the greatest common factor.
6.NS.6.at: Find the greatest common factor of any two whole numbers less than or equal to 100 and the least common multiple of any two whole numbers less than or equal to 12. Apply the distributive property to write an equivalent expression for the sum of two whole numbers using a multiple of the sum.
6.NS.6.above: Solve a real-world problem using the greatest common factor or least common multiple.

6.NS.7.below: Identify and name a variable, coefficient, constant, and term within a given algebraic expression, OR combine like terms or decompose a term to write or identify equivalent expressions.
6.NS.7.approaching: Apply the associative or commutative properties to identify or write equivalent expressions.
6.NS.7.at: Apply the distributive property to create or identify equivalent expressions. Apply a combination of properties, combining like terms, or decomposing terms to identify or write equivalent expressions. Justify whether two expressions are equivalent using substitution
6.NS.7.above: Apply properties of operations, combining like terms, or decomposing terms to write multiple equivalent expressions.

6.NS.8.below: Determine the relationship between the base and exponent in an exponential expression.
6.NS.8.approaching: Identify or write an equivalent expression to a given exponential expression with a rational base and a whole number exponent.
6.NS.8.at: Evaluate an exponential expression with a rational base and a whole number exponent.
6.NS.8.above: Analyze an error made when evaluating an exponential expression with a positive rational number base.

6.RP.1.below: Identify equivalent fractions, decimals and percents using a given model.
6.RP.1.approaching: Identify or write the equivalent conversion of a positive rational number in one way.
6.RP.1.at: Identify or write the equivalent conversions of a positive rational number in more than one way.
6.RP.1.above: Apply knowledge of equivalent forms of positive rational numbers to justify conversions.

6.RP.2.below: Identify a unit rate in a real-world context.
6.RP.2.approaching: Determine the unit rate when given a ratio or a ratio relationship expressed as a model.
6.RP.2.at: Calculate a rate using a given unit rate, or conversely, calculate a unit rate using a given rate within a real-world situation.
6.RP.2.above: Apply knowledge of unit rates and rates to reason through, critique, and justify steps to solving a problem.

6.RP.3.below: Identify ratios in real-world context and determine if they represent part-to-part or part-to-whole; OR identify or write equivalent ratios.
6.RP.3.approaching: Calculate the ratio represented in a table of values and determine missing values; OR plot pairs of values from a ratio table on a coordinate plane.
6.RP.3.at: Solve mathematical or real-world problems using a table or graph that represents equivalent ratios; OR construct an equivalent table of ratios when given a ratio.
6.RP.3.above: Analyze errors when creating a table of equivalent ratios or plotting ratios on a coordinate plane; OR compare and contrast ratios when given two or more different ratio tables.

6.RP.4.below: Identify a model that represents a real-world or mathematical ratio problem.
6.RP.4.approaching: Solve a real-world or mathematical rate or ratio problem given a model.
6.RP.4.at: Solve a real-world ratio problem using any ratio model or strategy; OR use ratios and ratio models to justify thinking.
6.RP.4.above: Compare two or more ratios to solve a real-world problem.

6.RP.5.below: Identify the independent and dependent variables in a real-world situation.
6.RP.5.approaching: Complete a table of values to represent a proportional relationship in a real-world situation; OR analyze the relationship between the independent and dependent values in a table to identify an equation expressing the dependent variable in terms of the independent variable.
6.RP.5.at: Analyze the relationship between the independent and dependent values of a real-world situation to write an equation and represent it graphically; OR solve real-world problems using the relationship between the independent and dependent variables.
6.RP.5.above: Critique statements made about a proportional relationship.

7.AF.1.below: Apply properties of operations as strategies to find missing values of equivalent linear expressions using addition and subtraction. Identify the correct steps in the process or the property applied.
7.AF.1.approaching: Apply properties of operations as strategies to identify equivalent linear expressions by factoring or applying the distributive property. Identify the correct steps in the process or the property applied.
7.AF.1.at: Apply properties of operations as strategies to construct equivalent linear expressions by factoring, expansion, and/or addition and subtraction. Justify each step in the process.
7.AF.1.above: Apply properties of operations as strategies to identify or create multiple equivalent linear expressions by factoring, expansion, or addition and subtraction. Justify each step in the process.

7.AF.2.below: Identify expressions or steps to solving real-world problems with rational numbers using one or two operations.
7.AF.2.approaching: Solve real-world problems with rational numbers using one operation.
7.AF.2.at: Solve real-world problems with rational numbers using two operations.
7.AF.2.above: Evaluate the reasoning or critique an argument involving generalizations and solutions to mathematical or real-world problems with rational numbers using two operations.

7.AF.3.below: Identify numbers as solutions to linear equations of the form px + q = r and p(x + q) = r, where p, q, and r are specific rational numbers.
7.AF.3.approaching: Solve equations of the form px + q = r and p(x + q) = r fluently, where p, q, and r are specific rational numbers; OR identify linear equations that represent a real-world problem.
7.AF.3.at: Represent and solve real-world problems leading to equations of the form px + q = r and p (x + q) = r where p, q, and r are rational numbers.
7.AF.3.above: Represent a real-world problem using more than one equation that simplifies to the form px + q = r and p (x + q) = r where p, q and r are rational numbers. Explain whether a solution to a given problem is reasonable. Compare an algebraic solution to an arithmetic solution, analyzing the sequence of the operations used in each approach.

7.AF.4.below: Solve inequalities of the form px + q > r or px + q < r, where p, q, and r are specific rational numbers, OR identify the correct graph of the solution to a given inequality.
7.AF.4.approaching: Solve inequalities of the form px + q ≥ r or px + q ≤ r, where p, q, and r are specific rational numbers, OR construct the correct graph of the solution to a given inequality.
7.AF.4.at: Solve real-world problems involving inequalities of the form px + q (> or ≥) r or px + q (< or ≤) r, where p, q, and r are rational numbers. Graph the solution set of the inequality and interpret it in the context of the problem.
7.AF.4.above: Critique a solution to a real-world problem for accuracy or reasonableness and justify arguments by applying understanding of inequalities.

7.AF.5.below: Analyze and classify graphs or tables as representing a constant or variable rate of change without computation. Interpret the meaning of slope as the amount of vertical change for each horizontal change.
7.AF.5.approaching: Analyze given situations to identify those that represent a constant rate of change modeled by a linear function or a varying rate of change.
7.AF.5.at: Analyze situations in context to determine if they model constant or varying rates of change resulting in linear or nonlinear functions and use reasoning about slope, rates of change, and linear functions to justify responses.
7.AF.5.above: Analyze the rate of change from a given situation or graph, including zero change. Interpret, explain, and/or compare various situations to determine if they can be modeled by a linear function.

7.AF.6.below: Determine if the slope of a given graph is positive, negative, 0, or undefined.
7.AF.6.approaching: Find the slope of a line given its graph.
7.AF.6.at: Graph a line given its slope and a point on the line.
7.AF.6.above: Determine the slope of a line in the context of a real-world situation. Identify additional points on a line when given the slope and one point.

7.DSP.1.below: Identify appropriate sampling that can be used to gain information about a population.
7.DSP.1.approaching: Identify whether a sampling method would be likely to produce a sample representative of a population; OR identify whether a sampling method is random or non-random.
7.DSP.1.at: Recognize whether a conclusion or generalization of a population based on a sample is valid based on the sampling method used.
7.DSP.1.above: Justify why a conclusion or generalization of a population based on a sample is or is not valid based on the sampling method used; OR Given a statistical question, design a sampling method that would be likely to produce a representative sample.

7.DSP.2.below: Calculate the mean, median, and range of numerical data from two random samples of populations to make comparisions.
7.DSP.2.approaching: Calculate the interquartile range and mean absolute deviation of numerical data from random samples of populations to make comparisons.
7.DSP.2.at: Make comparisons between two data sets from two populations using measures of central tendency (mean and median) and measures of spread (range, interquartile range, and mean absolute deviation) in real-world contexts.
7.DSP.2.above: Make, justify, and critique comparative inferences about two populations based on the comparison and interpretation of measures of central tendency (mean and median) and measures of spread (range, interquartile range, and mean absolute deviation).

7.DSP.3.below: Classify the visual overlap of two data sets as full, partial, or no overlap; OR identify sets of data that have the most overlap.
7.DSP.3.approaching: Analyze and make observations about the degree of visual overlap of two data sets represented as box plots using measures of center (mean and median) and spread (range, interquartile range, and mean absolute deviation).
7.DSP.3.at: Analyze and make observations about the degree of visual overlap of two data sets represented as line plots using measures of center (mean and median) and spread (range, interquartile range, and mean absolute deviation); OR describe how additional data points, including outliers, may affect the mean and/or median of a data set.
7.DSP.3.above: Make, justify, and critique comparative inferences about two populations based on the overlap of two numerical data distributions represented in line plots or box plots.

7.DSP.4.below: Classify the likelihood of one event occurring as either impossible, unlikely, equally likely, likely, or certain based on a given probability of 0, 1/2 or 1.
7.DSP.4.approaching: Classify the likelihood of each event from a given situation occurring as either impossible, unlikely, equally likely, likely, or certain.
7.DSP.4.at: Classify probabilities of events represented as fractions as impossible, unlikely, equally likely, likely, or certain.
7.DSP.4.above: Compare the likelihood of events given the probabilities of the events.

7.DSP.5.below: Represent the probability of an event in a sample space where n events are equally likely as 1/n, OR create a sample space for a simple experiment.
7.DSP.5.approaching: Represent the probability of an event as the ratio of the number of desired outcomes to the number of total outcomes in the sample space, given the sample space, OR
7.DSP.5.at: Represent the probability of an event as the ratio of the number of desired outcomes to the number of total outcomes in the sample space, given a description of the sample space. Create a probability model, given the sample space or a description of the sample space. Use a probability model to predict the approximate relative frequency of an event.
7.DSP.5.above: Compare probabilities of a probability model to observed frequencies and explain reasons for any differences between the two quantities.

7.GM.1.below: Identify the scale factor of a smaller figure to a larger figure when given scale drawings of geometric figures.
7.GM.1.approaching: Solve problems using a scale drawing of a geometric figure given the scale factor.
7.GM.1.at: Solve problems involving scale drawings of geometric figures, such as computing actual lengths and areas from a scale drawing and reproducing a scale drawing at a different scale. Justify scale drawings using proportional reasoning.
7.GM.1.above: Solve problems that involve applying multiple scale factors and justify scale drawings using proportional reasoning.

7.GM.2.below: Calculate the area or circumference of a circle, given the radius or diameter.
7.GM.2.approaching: Calculate the radius, diameter, or area given the circumference of a circle; OR calculate the radius, diameter, or circumference given the area of a circle in terms of π.
7.GM.2.at: Apply the formulas for the area and circumference of a circle to solve problems.
7.GM.2.above: Apply knowledge of the area and circumference of a circle or the informal derivation of the relationship between the two to solve complex problems.

7.GM.3.below: Calculate the volume of cylinders and three-dimensional objects composed of right rectangular prisms in a mathematical problem.
7.GM.3.approaching: Calculate the height or radius of a cylinder when given the volume of the cylinder and one other measurement; OR calculate a missing side length of a three-dimensional object composed of right rectangular prisms.
7.GM.3.at: Solve real-world and other mathematical problems involving finding the volume of cylinders and three-dimensional objects composed of right rectangular prisms.
7.GM.3.above: Solve real-world and other mathematical problems involving calculating the height or radius of a cylinder or calculating a missing side length of a three-dimensional object composed of right rectangular prisms.

7.NS.1.below: Identify and write the opposite of a number plotted on a given number line and use this understanding to find number pairs that sum to zero, including in simple real-world situations.
7.NS.1.approaching: Determine when two numbers on a number line sum to zero and identify or write expressions that represent this relationship. Calculate sums of positive and negative integers or decimals on a number line or solve simple real-world problems using these sums
7.NS.1.at: Calculate the sum of two positive and negative numbers and/or interpret the results by describing real-world situations. Explain how a number line can be used to add rational numbers. Identify or write expressions that represent the distance between a positive and negative number as the absolute value of their difference
7.NS.1.above: Reason about generalizations of adding positive and negative numbers when given an addition expression or a number line.

7.NS.2.below: Identify or write the absolute value of a given number. Calculate the distance between given integers plotted on a labeled number line to solve simple real-world problems.
7.NS.2.approaching: Identify expressions that represent the distance between a positive and negative number as the absolute value of their difference. Calculate the difference between positive and negative integers or decimals on a number line or solve simple real-world problems using these differences.
7.NS.2.at: Calculate the difference between rational numbers and/or interpret the results by describing real-world situations. Explain how a number line can be used to subtract rational numbers. Identify or write expressions that represent the distance between a positive and negative number as the absolute value of their difference
7.NS.2.above: Reason about generalizations of subtracting positive and negative numbers when given a subtraction expression or a number line.

7.NS.3.below: Multiply two integers or simple rational numbers with opposite signs using a model. Determine whether a multiplication expression with two or three rational numbers will result in a positive or negative product.
7.NS.3.approaching: Apply properties to multiply two or three rational numbers without the use of a model. Apply the distributive property to integer expressions involving a coefficient multiplied by a sum or difference. Apply the distributive property to simplify expressions with integers and evaluate numerical expressions that include addition and subtraction inside parentheses with an integer coefficient; identify equivalent expressions.
7.NS.3.at: Apply the distributive property to simplify expressions with rational numbers. Evaluate numerical expressions written as a coefficient multiplied by a sum or difference.
7.NS.3.above: Identify, generate, and justify multiple equivalent expressions with rational numbers and variables using the properties of operations and the rules for multiplying signed numbers. Analyze and generalize the sign and magnitude of products of rational numbers and variable expressions. Determine whether a product is greater than, less than, or equal to zero and select or construct inequalities that accurately represent the product.

7.NS.4.below: Identify equivalent fractions that satisfy –(p/q) = (–p)/q = p/(–q) when p and q are integers in tasks that do not require simplification. Identify the sign of the quotient when dividing two rational numbers in straightforward cases.
7.NS.4.approaching: Generate an equivalent fraction that satisfies the sign property when p and q are integers. Identify equivalent fractions that satisfy the sign properties when p and q are integers. Calculate the quotient of two rational numbers using a model.
7.NS.4.at: Identify equivalent fractions that satisfy the sign properties when p and q are integers in tasks that require simplification. Calculate the quotient of two rational numbers using properties of operations or rules for dividing signed numbers.
7.NS.4.above: Generate or identify multiple equivalent fractions representing negative rational numbers, including expressions with variables, double negatives, and non-simplified forms that require careful sign interpretation. Determine or justify the missing value in an equivalence statement involving negative rational numbers (including variable forms) and explain the reasoning used to verify equivalency.

7.NS.5.below: Classify numbers as either prime or composite. Identify the correct prime factorization of whole numbers that are multiples of 10 using only the prime numbers 2, 3, and 5 when provided options fully simplified into prime factors. Find a missing factor in a prime factorization equality statement when all factors are 2, 3, or 5.
7.NS.5.approaching: Identify the prime factorization of whole numbers less than 225, including numbers that are not multiples of 10, when given options that are not fully simplified into prime factors. Determine the missing exponent in a prime factorization expression. Identify equivalent prime factorization forms, using primes up to 7 and exponents of 3 or less.
7.NS.5.at: Generate the prime factorization of whole numbers. Determine the value of variables in an exponential expression when given the numerical value of the product.
7.NS.5.above: Analyze and justify the accuracy of a prime factorization expressed with exponents, including factorizations involving multi‑step decomposition of whole numbers 225 or greater.

7.NS.6.below: Identify numbers that are perfect squares. Calculate square roots of perfect square whole numbers less than or equal to 144. Represent the inverse relationship between squaring and square rooting symbolically using numbers or variables in simple expressions.
7.NS.6.approaching: Calculate square roots of perfect square whole numbers and identify or write equivalent expressions involving square roots and squared numbers using the inverse relationship, including values between 144 and 400. Apply the inverse relationship between squaring and square roots to determine up to two equivalent expressions for a given whole-number value.
7.NS.6.at: Find negative square roots of perfect squares. Determine missing values in equality statements involving square roots and squared numbers. Distinguish accurate equivalent expressions from incorrect forms.
7.NS.6.above: Apply the inverse relationship between squaring and square roots to evaluate, compare, or generate complex expressions involving radicals, exponents, and variables and justify the reasoning used. Analyze statements involving squared numbers and square roots to determine missing values or verify correctness, providing an explanation that clearly connects each step to the inverse relationship.

7.NS.7.below: Compute fluently with integers using an algorithmic approach.
7.NS.7.approaching: Compute fluently with integers and decimals using an algorithmic approach.
7.NS.7.at: Compute fluently with rational numbers using an algorithmic approach.
7.NS.7.above: Identify one or more equivalent expressions when one expression is given.

7.RP.1.below: Identify whether two quantities are in a proportional relationship.
7.RP.1.approaching: Identify a unit rate or constant of proportionality given a verbal description, table, or graph with the pair (1, r) included as an entry in the table or point on the graph.
7.RP.1.at: Calculate a unit rate or constant of proportionality given tables, graphs, equations, or verbal descriptions.
7.RP.1.above: Interpret the unit rate or constant of proportionality given a table, graph, equation or a verbal description of a proportional relationship in context. Use the unit rate or constant of proportionality to solve problems or make predictions in context.

7.RP.2.below: Use multiplication or addition to find missing ratio values in simple mathematical problems involving ratio or percent.
7.RP.2.approaching: Analyze and apply proportional relationships to solve simple real-world and mathematical problems, including simple ratio/percent problems.
7.RP.2.at: Analyze and apply proportional relationships to solve more complex or multi-step real-world and mathematical problems.
7.RP.2.above: Analyze and apply proportional relationships to solve complex real-world and mathematical problems, including working backwards problems to find the original cost/value.

7.RP.3.below: Write an equation to represent a proportional relationship given a verbal description.
7.RP.3.approaching: Identify or write an equation to represent a real-world or mathematical proportional relationship given a table or graph that includes the ordered pair that correlates to the constant of proportionality; OR draw graphs of proportional relationships given a table that includes the ordered pair that correlates to the constant of proportionality.
7.RP.3.at: Write an equation to represent a real-world or mathematical proportional relationship given a table or graph with non-consecutive values or coordinates and does not include the ordered pair that correlates to the constant of proportionality; OR draw graphs to represent proportional relationships, given an equation, table, or verbal description where the constant of proportionality must be calculated.
7.RP.3.above: Explain and interpret an equation that represents a proportional relationship to make predictions or draw conclusions.

8.AF.1.below: Determine whether a given number is a solution to a linear equation or inequality.
8.AF.1.approaching: Solve linear equations and inequalities in one variable with rational number coefficients, including solutions that require expanding expressions using the distributive property and collecting like terms on one side of the equation or inequality.
8.AF.1.at: Create and solve linear equations and inequalities in one variable with rational number coefficients, including solutions that require expanding expressions using the distributive property and collecting like terms on one side of the equation or inequality to solve real-world problems.
8.AF.1.above: Use complex linear equations and inequalities to solve real-world problems and justify solutions.

8.AF.2.below: Classify one equation as having one solution, infinitely many solutions, or no solutions when given a linear equation and its solution.
8.AF.2.approaching: Classify one or more linear equations as having one solution, infinitely many solutions, or no solutions when given equations that do not require simplification.
8.AF.2.at: Generate a linear equation that has one solution, infinitely many solutions, or no solutions. Classify one or more linear equations that require simplification on one or both sides of the equation as having one solution, infinitely many solutions, or no solutions.
8.AF.2.above: Analyze and justify a claim about the number of solutions to a multi-step linear equation.

8.AF.3.below: Identify the independent and dependent variables given a table, graph, or set of ordered pairs.
8.AF.3.approaching: Define the meaning of a function, OR identify characteristics of a function using a set of ordered pairs.
8.AF.3.at: Apply understanding of functions to determine if a relation is a function or nonfunction.
8.AF.3.above: Explain whether a given representation of a relation in a real-world situation is a function or is not a function: OR critique an explanation determining if a relation in any form is a function.

8.AF.4.below: Identify a qualitative description given a graph, or a graph given a qualitative description, with no context.
8.AF.4.approaching: Identify a qualitative description given a graph, or a graph given a qualitative description, within a context.
8.AF.4.at: Construct the graph of a function that matches a given qualitative description.
8.AF.4.above: Use knowledge of qualitative descriptions to interpret and draw conclusions about given graphs within context, OR sketch a graph of a function given qualitative data in the form of real-world data in context.

8.AF.5.below: Interpret the slope and y-intercept from a linear equation given in slope-intercept form (y = mx + b).
8.AF.5.approaching: Classify given equations as linear or non-linear.
8.AF.5.at: Compare functions in similar and different representations using properties of functions to determine if they are linear or nonlinear.
8.AF.5.above: Interpret and explain characteristics of linear or nonlinear functions as they apply to real-world situations.

8.AF.6.below: Determine the rate of change or y-intercept of a linear function represented by a table, graph, or verbal description.
8.AF.6.approaching: Identify an equation of a linear function represented by a table, graph, or verbal description.
8.AF.6.at: Construct a linear function when given a verbal description, table, or graph, and interpret the rate of change or y-intercept of a linear function in terms of the situation it models. Graph a linear equation presented in slope-intercept form.
8.AF.6.above: Interpret how the values of the two quantities change together within a given linear function in context. Interpret the rate of change and initial value of a linear function in terms of the situation it models, its graph, or its table of values.

8.AF.7.below: Given a linear function, identify an equivalent function in a different form.
8.AF.7.approaching: Compare properties of two functions each represented in the same way (algebraically, graphically, numerically in tables, or by verbal descriptions).
8.AF.7.at: Compare properties of two functions, each represented in a different way (algebraically, graphically, numerically in tables, or by verbal descriptions).
8.AF.7.above: Create a different representation of a linear function that has a greater or lesser slope and y-intercept.

8.AF.8.below: Determine the number of solutions a system has when given a system of equations represented graphically.
8.AF.8.approaching: Determine or approximate the solution to a system of equations when given a system of equations represented graphically.
8.AF.8.at: Graph a system of equations and determine or approximate the solution.
8.AF.8.above: Interpret or solve real-world problems by estimating solutions to systems of equations.

8.DSP.1.below: Accurately identify positive, negative, or no association between two quantities using a scatter plot.
8.DSP.1.approaching: Identify more than one characteristic of a data set, such as outliers, positive or negative association, linear association, and nonlinear association.
8.DSP.1.at: Construct and interpret scatter plots for bivariate measurement data to investigate patterns of association between two quantities, AND describe patterns such as clustering, outliers, positive or negative association, linear association, and nonlinear association.
8.DSP.1.above: Analyze patterns of association between two quantities and use data to critique responses; OR create a scatter plot to represent given descriptors.

8.DSP.2.below: Interpret the slope and y-intercept of a line of best fit, with slope and/or intercept parameter identified, in terms of the context.
8.DSP.2.approaching: Interpret the slope and intercept of a modeling equation in terms of the context.
8.DSP.2.at: Solve problems about the slope and intercept of a line of best fit in terms of the context.
8.DSP.2.above: Justify the reasonableness of the predictions in the context of the bivariate measurement data.

8.DSP.3.below: Identify the correct sample space for a given compound event.
8.DSP.3.approaching: Calculate the probability of a compound, independent event using any strategy; OR identify an outcome missing from a sample space of a given compound event.
8.DSP.3.at: Calculate the probability of a compound, dependent event using any strategy.
8.DSP.3.above: Find the probability of a compound event that consists of an independent event and dependent event.

8.DSP.4.below: Given a description of an event, determine whether it is independent, dependent, complementary, or mutually exclusive.
8.DSP.4.approaching: Identify an expression that uses fractions to represent the outcome of a compound event.
8.DSP.4.at: Calculate the probability of an event given a description. Explain the probability of a given event in terms of a fraction of outcomes in the sample space.
8.DSP.4.above: Analyze an error made when calculating the probability of a compound event given a verbal description. Compare the probability of two or more events given a verbal description.

8.DSP.5.below: Demonstrate how the multiplication counting principle can be used to find the same number of outcomes as a listing method.
8.DSP.5.approaching: Identify or write expressions to represent the application of the multiplication counting principle to small-scale situations; OR solve small-scale problems by applying the multiplication counting principle.
8.DSP.5.at: Solve large-scale problems by applying the multiplication counting principle.
8.DSP.5.above: Solve problems that include constraints on order or repetition by applying the multiplication counting principle.

8.GM.1.below: Identify the type of transformation used to create a similar figure on a given coordinate plane.
8.GM.1.approaching: Identify the coordinates of a point or the specific transformation performed on a preimage to result in an image.
8.GM.1.at: Perform a single transformation (dilation, translation, rotation, or reflection) using given information and determine the coordinates of the new figure.
8.GM.1.above: Perform a multi-step transformation using a combination of dilations, translations, rotations, and reflections on a coordinate plane; OR analyze the new figure to determine the effects of the transformation on the attributes of the figure.

8.GM.2.below: Calculate the volume of cones, spheres, and pyramids and the surface area of spheres in a mathematical problem.
8.GM.2.approaching: Calculate missing dimensions of cones and pyramids using the formulas for volume or surface area.
8.GM.2.at: Solve real-world problems by applying the formulas for the volume of cones, spheres, or pyramids or the surface area of a sphere. Justify solutions.
8.GM.2.above: Apply the volume formulas of cones, spheres, and pyramids to solve real-world and mathematical problems in which the volume of one shape must be used to determine the volume of another shape. Apply the surface area formula of a sphere to find the volume of the sphere.

8.GM.3.below: Identify or write the Pythagorean Theorem for a given triangle.
8.GM.3.approaching: Apply the Pythagorean Theorem to calculate an unknown length of a right triangle in real-world or other mathematical problems in two dimensions.
8.GM.3.at: Apply the Pythagorean Theorem to determine unknown side lengths of right triangles to solve real-world problems.
8.GM.3.above: Apply the Pythagorean Theorem to solve real-world and mathematical problems involving two- and three-dimensional shapes composed of at least one right triangle.

8.NS.1.below: Classify given numbers as rational or irrational.
8.NS.1.approaching: Convert given fractions into decimals and classify them as terminating, or repeating; OR convert a repeating decimal into a rational number.
8.NS.1.at: Classify a given number as rational or irrational and justify the reasoning for each classification.
8.NS.1.above: Analyze, justify, and apply reasoning to prove or disprove a generalization about rational or irrational numbers.

8.NS.2.below: Plot rational approximations of irrational numbers on a number line. Identify an irrational number that is greater than or less than a given whole number. Identify the approximate value to the nearest whole number of an irrational number.
8.NS.2.approaching: Identify approximated values of irrational numbers to the nearest tenth, including those with a numerical operation in the radicand, requiring simplification prior to approximation. Compare irrational numbers within intervals.
8.NS.2.at: Compare a rational number and a rational approximation of an irrational number in the form radical (k) or k*pi, using inequalities, number lines, or verbal statements. Determine rational and/or irrational numbers that meet given comparison requirements.
8.NS.2.above: Analyze and compare values using rational approximations of complex irrational expressions and large non-perfect square radicals. Order sets of rational and irrational numbers from least to greatest and justify comparisons.

8.NS.3.below: Apply the product of powers, power of a power, and negative exponent properties to identify equivalent, fully simplified numerical expressions using integer bases and exponents. Identify unknown exponents in simple equality statements involving a single exponent property.
8.NS.3.approaching: Apply the product of powers, power of a power, negative exponent, and quotient of powers properties to generate or identify equivalent expressions, including expressions that are not fully simplified. Determine missing exponents in simple equality statements involving two properties.
8.NS.3.at: Apply the product of powers, power of a power, negative exponent, quotient of powers, and zero exponent properties to generate or identify equivalent expressions, including those with fractional bases. Find missing exponents in complex expressions. Simplify expressions involving negative integers in the quotient property.
8.NS.3.above: Apply multiple exponent properties flexibly to analyze, compare, and generate more than two equivalent expressions. Find the value of more than one missing exponent.

8.NS.4.below: Identify expressions or steps to solving real-world problems with rational numbers and two or more steps.
8.NS.4.approaching: Determine solutions to simple real-world problems that involve rational numbers by recognizing operations, including applying one percent calculation or unit conversion.
8.NS.4.at: Determine solutions to real-world problems involving multiple operations with rational numbers that require selecting operations based on the structure of the content and integrating percent reasoning with multiple steps. Solve complex real-world problems involving rational numbers that require interpreting signed values, combining multiple operations, and applying percent reasoning or conversions in the appropriate order.
8.NS.4.above: Determine solutions to complex real-world problems involving multiple operations with rational numbers that require advanced reasoning with percentages. Solve extended real-world problems involving rational numbers that require integrating signed quantities, multi-step percent changes (including repeated or negative percents), additive or multiplicative adjustments, and selective conversions to produce and compare accurate final values.
